title: You almost missed it.
paragraphs: You almost missed it.

Not the obvious sin. Not the loud rebellion.
Something quieter. Stranger.
It was hiding in the aftermath… in what should have been dead.
A man reached into the carcass of a lion—and found honey.
Read that again.
In Book of Judges 14, the story slips by fast. Samson tears apart a lion with his bare hands. No weapon. Just raw, God-given strength. Then he walks away.
Days later, he comes back.
The lion is still there. Rotting. Hollowed out.
And inside that death… something is alive.
“Behold, a swarm of bees and honey were in the body of the lion.” (Judges 14:8)
That doesn’t make sense.
Honey doesn’t come from death.
Sweetness doesn’t grow inside what was torn, broken, and abandoned.
But there it was.
And if you’re honest, this is where your story starts to feel uncomfortable.
Because you’ve been trying to pretend that your past is just… dead.
That what happened—what you did, what was done to you, what you became in those hidden moments—doesn’t still sit there, waiting.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
God doesn’t waste dead things.
You thought that season killed you.

The addiction.
The secret relationship.
The compromise you swore you’d never make.
The nights where conviction knocked—and you locked the door.
God saw it.
You knew.
And now you carry it like a carcass you refuse to revisit.
But what if the place you’re avoiding is exactly where God hid something?
Not to justify the sin. Never that.
The lion was still a lion. It still attacked. It still needed to be destroyed.
Sin is still sin.
“For the wages of sin is death…” (Romans 6:23)
Not weakness. Not “mistakes.”
Death.
That thing you played with… it killed something in you.

Your peace.
Your clarity.
Your sensitivity to God’s voice.
And you felt it.
That dullness. That distance.
Where prayer felt mechanical. Where Scripture felt silent. Where worship felt like pretending.
You told yourself it was just a phase.
But deep down…
You knew something had died.
And this is where the story splits.
Because most people stop there.
They live the rest of their lives circling the carcass, either pretending it isn’t there… or being haunted by it.
But Samson went back.
Not to relive the fight.
To face what remained.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
And when he did, he found something no one expects to come from death.
Sweetness.
This is the part religion often gets wrong.
It tells you to clean yourself up first. To fix what’s broken. To earn your way back.
But Scripture says something completely different.
“God demonstrates His own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
Not after you fixed it.
Not after you explained it.
While you were still in it.
Jesus didn’t avoid your dead places.
He stepped into them.
The cross wasn’t clean.
It was brutal. Public. Bloody.
It looked like total defeat.
And yet…
That is where grace was born.
“But the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 6:23)
Sweetness… from death.
You keep thinking your story disqualifies you.
That what you’ve done has ruined any chance of real transformation.
But the Gospel doesn’t deny the carcass.
It transforms what comes out of it.
Not by your effort.
By His sacrifice.
This is where it gets personal.
Because some of you are still holding onto the honey… but refusing to acknowledge where it came from.
You like the idea of grace.
You like the comfort, the encouragement, the hope.
But you don’t want to confront the lion.
You don’t want to call sin what it is.
You don’t want repentance—you want relief.
And those are not the same thing.
“Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out.” (Acts 3:19)
Repentance is not shame.
It’s surrender.
It’s turning around and saying, “God, I was wrong. Not partially. Completely.”
No excuses.
No edits.
Just truth.
And that’s where the sweetness actually begins.
Not in denial.
In honesty.
Because when you finally stop protecting your sin… you make room for grace to do what it was meant to do.
To cleanse.
To restore.
To make something new.
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)
Not improved.
New.
But you don’t get resurrection without death.
You don’t get honey without the lion.
And you don’t get transformation without the cross.
So here you are.
Standing between two choices.
Or…
You can go back.
Not to stay there.
But to face it with God.
To let Him show you what He’s been doing in places you thought were wasted.
To finally surrender the part of your life you’ve been managing instead of repenting from.
Say it.
Even if it’s uncomfortable.
Even if it exposes you.
Type it out: “I’ve been avoiding what God wants to redeem.”
Not for me.
For you.
And if someone came to mind while you were reading this—the one who’s still stuck in their past, still believing they’re too far gone—send this to them.
Don’t overthink it.
This is how light spreads.
Stay here if you’re ready to go deeper.
Not just inspiration—but correction, growth, real discipleship rooted in Scripture.
That’s what’s waiting for you:
Because the story doesn’t end at the carcass.
And it doesn’t even end at the honey.
There’s something else God was doing in Samson’s life… something most people never see until it’s too late.
